claim: In a randomized trial of 50 UK intelligence analysts, ACH training did not improve probability accuracy; the untrained control was slightly better (MAE 0.26 vs 0.21, random guessing 0.33).
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Do not run ACH as a default step; any ACH-like step must be measured against plain voting at equal calls.

claim: ACH and control analysts both gave incoherent probabilities: the four mutually exclusive hypotheses summed to 1.77 (ACH) and 1.54 (control) instead of 1.0.
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Whenever the agent outputs probabilities over exclusive options, normalize them in code; unpacking inflates totals.

claim: Statistical repair beat the method: coherentizing cut MAE from 0.23 to 0.15 (35%), and coherentizing plus equal-weight averaging of all 50 analysts cut it to 0.09 (61%). Simple normalization gave 0.13, slightly better than coherentization. Coherence weighting did not beat equal weighting.
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: Program step: normalize to sum 1, then equal-weight average several varied-prompt calls. Test whether same-model samples give the same gain.

claim: ACH-trained analysts rated the usefulness of cues much closer to true probability gain (r=.68 vs .17 control), but this did not improve final accuracy.
title: Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
transfer: A diagnosticity score is learnable but must be wired into the final decision by code, not left to the model's last step.

claim: ACH-trained analysts did not follow all ACH steps; evidence on confirmation bias was mixed; ACH may raise inconsistency and error.
quote: ACH-trained analysts did not follow all of the steps of ACH.
title: The analysis of competing hypotheses in intelligence analysis
transfer: A program does not skip steps, so a human null does not prove an agent null. Log step completion anyway.

claim: In 227 participants judging 6 cases with uncertain evidence, ACH gave no coherence advantage and was slightly less reliable on matched pairs (MAD .22 vs .18, p=.051, d=0.20).
title: Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
transfer: Expect ACH-style scoring to add noise; compare against a no-matrix control.

claim: ACH users let non-diagnostic evidence move judgments by about 30-32% of the effect of perfectly diagnostic evidence (pseudo-diagnostic weighting); all participants were also conservative, staying near 50/50.
title: Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
transfer: In any evidence matrix, code must drop cells marked consistent with all hypotheses instead of letting the model weigh them.

claim: Dhami 2024 (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications) reportedly studies ACH matrix layout and confirmation bias; the page redirected to a login and I could not read it, so the finding rests on the earlier brief only.
title: unconfirmed (DOI 10.1186/s41235-024-00560-y)
transfer: Possible prompt-layout A/B (hypotheses by evidence table vs prose). Do not cite until read.

claim: Eleven LLMs in a Wason 2-4-6 style task often propose tests that confirm their hypothesis; counterexample-style prompts raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average, and distilling the behavior transferred to the Blicket test.
quote: the tendency to seek evidence that supports rather than challenges one's belief
title: Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
transfer: In hypothesis-testing loops with feedback, force the agent to propose a test whose outcome could refute its leader.

claim: Correction to the earlier brief: arXiv 2609.00738 is 'Escaping Reasoning Basin Collapse with History-Biased Search' (BASIN, single author Lu Cheng, NeurIPS'26), not a structure-aware MuSR paper. It beats Tree of Thoughts by up to +22 pp on Game of 24 and +6.7 pp on MuSR at matched budget.
title: Escaping Reasoning Basin Collapse with History-Biased Search
transfer: Penalize revisiting the same reasoning basin: cluster candidate lines and shift budget to unexplored clusters, as a diversity step.

claim: An evidence-first troubleshooting agent (SIA) keeps competing hypotheses, a counterfactual challenger and cited evidence records; it is tested on 303 forum threads in 3 domains against direct, reasoning, ReAct and ToT baselines. The abstract gives no numeric results.
quote: multiple causes can explain the same symptoms
title: LLM-as-an-Investigator: Evidence-First Agentic Reasoning for Robust Interactive Problem Diagnosis
transfer: Closest published analog to an ACH-lite agent: shared hypothesis and evidence state plus a counterfactual challenger. Read full results before relying on it.

claim: GPT-4 multi-agent conversations on 16 bias-caused misdiagnosis cases raised top-differential accuracy from 0% (0/80) initially to 71.3% (57/80). Simulated cases, no human baseline.
title: Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy through Multi-Agent Conversations: Using LLMs to Mitigate Cognitive Bias
transfer: On open diagnosis tasks where the first answer is biased, a critic role can help; the 0% start is selected for bias, so it overstates general gains.

claim: A preregistered study of 991 people found LLM assistants raised forecasting accuracy by 24-28% over control, even when one assistant was deliberately overconfident and noisy.
title: AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
transfer: LLM advice as one input among others helps humans; for an agent, treat its own advice as a signal to aggregate, not to trust.

claim: An LLM forecasting system with agentic news search, a supervisor that reconciles several forecasts, and statistical calibration matches human superforecasters on ForecastBench.
title: AIA Forecaster: Technical Report
transfer: Pipeline shape matches intelligence practice: independent forecasts, a reconciler, then calibration in code.

claim: Claim that standard multi-agent debate cannot improve on majority voting because correlated errors reinforce consensus mistakes; a peer-prediction method (AceMAD) is proposed.
title: Breaking the Martingale Curse: Multi-Agent Debate via Asymmetric Cognitive Potential Energy
transfer: Same-model agreement is weak evidence; a red-team call by the same model should not count as an independent vote.

claim: In multi-agent debate, about one in four divergent cases had the correct answer held by the minority, which majority voting suppresses; a classifier reached 81.2% flip precision for when to overturn the majority.
title: Minority Sentinel: When to Overturn Majority Voting in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
transfer: On a split, keep the minority answer alive and test it, rather than outvoting it.

claim: Across seven decision protocols in multi-agent debate, voting improved reasoning tasks by 13.2% and consensus improved knowledge tasks by 2.8%, so the best aggregation depends on task type.
title: Voting or Consensus? Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Debate
transfer: Route aggregation by task type: vote on reasoning, deliberate on knowledge.

claim: All tested LLMs conform to majority responses, more so when uncertain; Devil's Advocate prompting is proposed as a mitigation.
title: Conformity in Large Language Models
transfer: Do not show an LLM judge the majority answer before its own judgment; keep calls blind to each other.

claim: A 48-person experiment (12 groups) found LLM devil's-advocate counterarguments raised satisfaction for all members, especially minority members; the rise in cognitive workload was not significant. No accuracy outcome is stated in the abstract.
title: Conversational Agents as Catalysts for Critical Thinking: Challenging Social Influence in Group Decision-making
transfer: Mostly relevant to a multiplayer product (people plus agent), not to single-agent accuracy.

claim: Anticipatory reflection ('devil's advocate' before acting) in a WebArena agent reached 23.5% success, 3.5 points above prior zero-shot methods, and cut trials and plan revisions by 45%.
title: Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents
transfer: Premortem step before an irreversible action: list how it could fail and adjust the plan once.

claim: Schwenk's 1990 meta-analysis of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry exists (OBHDP 47(1):161-176), but the record page had no abstract and the full text was paywalled, so effect sizes remain unread.
title: Effects of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry on decision making: A meta-analysis
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
transfer: none until effect sizes are read

claim: Search gap: the arXiv API returned zero entries for 'structured analytic techniques', and I found no LLM paper that tests a full ACH matrix, key assumptions check or red team against a plain baseline. WebSearch was unavailable (session budget used up), so this is a limit of my search, not proof of absence.
title: Negative search result
transfer: An ACH-lite versus majority vote test on our own split cases is an open, cheap experiment.
